# Incident Report — Malware Infection, Host 192.168.1.216
**Case reference:** mta-2022-01-07 packet capture analysis
**Capture window:** 2022-01-07 20:04:09 to 20:16:40 (capture-local time), ~5,880 frames

## 1. Infected Host

| Attribute | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **192.168.1.216** | Source of all malicious HTTP POSTs, DHCP request |
| MAC address | **9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9** (ASUSTek NIC) | Ethernet source on the DHCP request and all traffic from .216 |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** | DHCP Option 12 hostname; confirmed via mDNS query `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2.local`, LLMNR query, and Kerberos principal `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2$` (NBNS shows a one-character transposition, `DESKTOP-GXNYNO2`, from a stale/legacy NetBIOS registration — DHCP and Kerberos are authoritative) |
| Logged-in domain user | **steve.smith** | Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ CNameString `steve.smith` from 192.168.1.216 to the domain controller 192.168.1.2 |
| Domain / DC | SPOONWATCH.NET, DC = SPOONWATCH-DC (192.168.1.2) | NBNS `SPOONWATCH-DC<20>`, DNS SRV lookups for `_ldap._tcp...spoonwatch.net` |

The gateway is 192.168.1.1 (Cisco NIC 1c:17:d3:f6:df:0a), consistent with a standard /24 enterprise LAN.

## 2. Malware Family

**Behavioral attribution only — not signature-confirmed.** No Suricata/IDS alert files were provided alongside the PCAP, and no hash-reputation lookup was performed (no internet access used, per instructions). The following traffic pattern was extracted directly from the capture:

- 192.168.1.216 opens one persistent HTTP/1.1 (Keep-Alive) TCP session to **2.56.57.108:80** at t=203s, connecting directly to the **raw IP with no preceding DNS lookup** — the C2 address is hardcoded, a common malware C2-evasion trait.
- Header fingerprint on every request: `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8`, `Accept-Charset: iso-8859-1, utf-8, utf-16, *;q=0.1`, no `User-Agent` header — a distinctive, non-browser HTTP client signature.
- The client POSTs a fixed 25-byte multipart/form-data body (an empty check-in beacon) to a sequence of paths under a **`/osk/` gate**: `6.jpg, 1.jpg, 2.jpg, 3.jpg, 4.jpg, 5.jpg, 7.jpg`. Each response is labeled `Content-Type: image/jpeg` but the payload is in fact a **Windows PE32 DLL** (`MZ` header, verified with `file`) — modules disguised as images to blend into web-proxy logs.
- It then POSTs to `/osk//main.php` (check-in/report, empty 200 response), followed by a final POST to `/osk/` carrying a **379,629-byte payload that is a ZIP archive** containing `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, and `passwords.txt` — i.e., harvested Chrome autofill data, saved credit-card data, cookies, and stored passwords being exfiltrated to the C2.

This is a modular loader/downloader that pulls multiple DLL payload stages disguised as JPEGs from a single hardcoded C2 and stages/exfiltrates a browser-credential-stealer archive over the same channel — a pattern most consistent with the **IcedID (BokBot) loader + stealer-module family**. This label is a behavioral judgment based on the traffic shape described above, not a hash/signature match against a known-malware database, since no such lookup was run.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the PCAP)

### Command-and-control
- **2.56.57.108:80/tcp** (HTTP, no domain used — connected by hardcoded IP)

### Malicious URLs (all on the C2 above)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//6.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//1.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//2.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//3.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//4.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//5.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//7.jpg` — module download (DLL)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//main.php` — check-in beacon
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk/` — stolen-data upload (POST, 379,629 bytes)

No malicious DNS domain was observed; all other DNS queries in the capture resolve to legitimate Microsoft telemetry/update infrastructure (`*.data.microsoft.com`, `*.windowsupdate.com`, `www.bing.com`, `api.msn.com`) and internal AD SRV records for `spoonwatch.net` — these are not part of the compromise.

### Transferred files and SHA256 hashes

| File (as served) | Type | Size (bytes) | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6.jpg` | PE32 DLL (GUI) | 144,848 | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| `1.jpg` | PE32 DLL (console) | 645,592 | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| `2.jpg` | PE32 DLL (GUI) | 334,288 | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| `3.jpg` | PE32 DLL (GUI) | 137,168 | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| `4.jpg` | PE32 DLL (console) | 440,120 | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| `5.jpg` | PE32 DLL (GUI) | 1,246,160 | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| `7.jpg` | PE32 DLL (console) | 83,784 | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |
| stolen-data upload (`POST /osk/` body) | ZIP archive (Chrome autofill/cc/cookies/passwords) | 379,629 | `1ecee6ff37e03c1160b8bf66d5ca8dc784e0b35fb9fd105f0964b314d310c07f` |

All other traffic in the capture (Kerberos/LDAP/SMB2/DCE-RPC to the DC, Windows Update .cab/.exe downloads from Microsoft CDN IPs 23.38.189.225/23.38.189.201/8.253.189.126, TLS sessions to Microsoft telemetry endpoints) is consistent with normal Windows domain-joined workstation behavior and shows no additional signs of compromise.

## 4. Summary

Host **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 (192.168.1.216, MAC 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9)**, logged in as domain user **steve.smith** on the **SPOONWATCH.NET** domain, is actively compromised. Malware on the host beacons to a hardcoded C2 at **2.56.57.108:80**, downloads seven DLL payload modules disguised as JPEG files under an `/osk/` gate, and exfiltrates a ZIP archive of stolen Chrome browser credentials, cookies, autofill data, and credit-card data back to the same C2. Family attribution (IcedID/BokBot-style loader+stealer) is behavioral, based on the traffic pattern, and should be confirmed with static/dynamic malware analysis of the recovered DLLs and hash lookups before being stated as confirmed in any external-facing report.
